**February 20, 1952 — a Wednesday**

You arrived in a year that felt, on the surface, like recovery — and was, underneath, full of things that hadn't yet gone wrong.

**Fourteen days before your birth — the world's most famous monarchy changed hands:** On February 6, King George VI died at Sandringham at 56, worn down by lung cancer and the strains of a wartime reign he had never expected to hold. His daughter Elizabeth was 25 and in Kenya when the news reached her. She came home as queen. The coronation was still 16 months away. You were born into the interregnum — the old king buried, the new queen not yet crowned. Elizabeth II would reign for 70 years, dying in September 2022 at 96. You were 70 years old. Her reign and your life are nearly congruent.

**Your birth year's hidden emergency — polio:** 1952 was the worst polio year in American history. Nearly 58,000 cases were reported; more than 3,200 people died; over 21,000 were left with some degree of paralysis. Swimming pools closed in summer. Parents kept children indoors. The fear was specific and physical — a virus that could take a healthy child and leave them in an iron lung before the week was out. You were an infant during the epidemic's peak. The Salk vaccine that ended the terror wasn't licensed until 1955, when you were 3. The casual confidence with which your own generation vaccinates children against diseases that once killed and maimed thousands is something your parents could not have imagined holding you that February.

**Your exact birthday, ten years forward:** On February 20, 1962 — your tenth birthday — John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. Friendship 7 lifted off from Cape Canaveral and completed three orbits in just under five hours before splashing down in the Atlantic. The space race, which had dominated your childhood, paused to celebrate on your birthday. The date is yours and Glenn's both.

**The election year you were born into:** 1952 was a presidential election year, and not a routine one. Truman, scarred by Korea and falling approval, chose not to run. The Democrats nominated Adlai Stevenson; the Republicans turned to Dwight Eisenhower, the general who had commanded the Allied forces in Europe. Eisenhower won in a landslide in November. The man who had overseen D-Day was now in the White House. The generation that fought the war was now governing the country its children — including you — would grow up in.

**The atomic clock ticking at your birth:** The United States tested its first thermonuclear weapon in November 1952, months after you were born — not an atomic bomb but a hydrogen bomb, with a yield roughly 450 times greater than the bomb that destroyed Hiroshima. The Soviet Union tested its own hydrogen bomb the following year. The arsenals that accumulated over the decades of your childhood and young adulthood grew large enough to end civilization many times over. That those arsenals were never used — and were partially dismantled before you turned 40 — is among the most improbable facts of your lifetime.

**The arc from 1952 to 74:** You were 11 when Kennedy was shot in Dallas. You were 17 when humans walked on the moon — the culmination of the space race whose American chapter launched on your tenth birthday. You were 37 when the Berlin Wall fell and the Cold War that had been the background condition of your entire life dissolved in weeks. You were 49 on September 11, 2001. You have watched television go from a novelty your parents marveled at to an antique medium; watched computing go from filling entire rooms to fitting in a shirt pocket; watched the global population more than double.

The Wednesday you were born, the new queen had not yet been crowned, the polio vaccine did not yet exist, and the hydrogen bomb was being assembled for its first test. The 74-year-old who carries that birthdate has outlived every one of those anxieties — and watched new ones take their place.
